summary: This snippet swaps the playlist's PriorityQueue from plain strings to Song objects, ordering them by their energyLevel from highest to lowest. Draining the queue with poll() plays the most energetic song first, no matter what order the songs were added in.

lines.text: A PriorityQueue of domain objects has no natural order to fall back on, so it must be handed a Comparator. comparingInt pulls the int out of each Song and orders it smallest first, and .reversed() flips that so the high-energy songs come off the front.
The songs are copied out of the existing playlist in one call, and each one sifts into position in the heap as it arrives. The original list is left untouched and still in its own order.

Reading a priority queue is destructive: the loop keeps going until the queue is empty because each poll() removes a song. Printing energyQueue directly would show the heap's internal layout, not a tidy high-to-low list.

lines.code: Song nextSong = energyQueue.poll(); // highest energy first
lines.text: poll() removes and returns the head, which under this comparator is always the highest-energy song remaining. Because the isEmpty() check guards the loop, poll() never returns null here.
Concatenating a Song into a string calls its toString(), which is why the Song class defines one — without it you would see a class name and a hash code.
